director.chapterArc: Arrival and surrender: Jab moves from exhausted survival mode into bureaucratic processing, culminating in the loss of his identity (the cord) and the acceptance of permanent displacement.
director.restraintNote: Maintain a flat, observational tone for narration. Character voices must be distinct but not caricatured; Otto is tired efficiency, Callie is detached observation, Hallet is procedural weariness. The emotional weight comes from Jab's silence and physical actions (counting paces, handing over the cord), not vocal inflection.

cues.delivery: Measured counting rhythm. Jab's head is occupied with the arithmetic of survival; keep pace steady and functional.
cues.from: Three hundred and forty paces, the girl had said, and Jab counted them, because his head would not do anything else.
cues.through: They went along the east shoulder in a line with two lamps, the big boy called Otto pulling a two-wheeled barrow with a folded blanket on the boards and a four-year-old lying on it, and the small woman walking at the barrow's head with one hand on the rim, not holding, only there. Jab walked at the side with his brother's hand in his.
cues.reason: Establishes the physical reality of arrival before dialogue begins.

cues.delivery: Otto's voice is tired but efficient. He speaks as a man who has been taught to say things; no emotional coloring.
cues.from: "How's the head end," said Otto, over his shoulder. He was very large and he was pulling with a strap over one shoulder and the far handle braced somewhere about his hip, and he said it the way a man says a thing he has been taught to say.
cues.through: "He's talking," said the small woman.
cues.reason: Differentiate Otto from Jab without making him overly sympathetic.

cues.delivery: Tonk's voice is immediate and factual. He asserts his state ('I'm not') with a four-year-old's directness.
cues.from: "I'm not," said Tonk.
cues.through: "There you are," she said. "He's talking."
cues.reason: Capture the child's specific reality without infantilizing him.

cues.delivery: Tonk observes the light with wonder but keeps it grounded. Jab's laugh is brief and tired.
cues.from: "It's got a light on it."
cues.through: "That's one," said Tonk, with the last of what he had, and Jab laughed, and somewhere ahead of them a slab of steel began to come open in the side of an earth bank with a flat white lamp burning over it in the middle of the night.
cues.reason: Contrast Tonk's immediate sensory experience with Jab's exhaustion.

cues.delivery: 'Clinical' is a tactical command. Jab speaks it louder to cut through the procedural noise; urgency without panic.
cues.from: "Clinical."
cues.through: "Clinical," said Jab, louder. "There's a boy on this barrow and he's four years old and it's clinical."
cues.reason: The word 'clinical' carries the weight of their survival strategy.

cues.delivery: Jab repeats with precision. He knows he has won a tactical victory; the voice is firm but not shouting.
cues.from: The grey coat nearest him turned his flat panel round. Jab could see his own face in it, small and grey and streaked with something.
cues.through: "Clinical," said Jab. "Now, and not after the boots."
cues.reason: Emphasize Jab's competence in using the correct terminology.

cues.delivery: The woman speaks with professional warmth but no sentimentality. Her tone is clinical even in greeting.
cues.from: "Hello, my love," she said. "What's your name?"
cues.through: "That's a very good name. I'm going to look at your leg and I'm not going to move it."
cues.reason: Establish her authority and lack of false comfort.

cues.delivery: Tonk states a fact. The woman's response is immediate and devoid of surprise.
cues.from: "It's broken," said Tonk.
cues.through: "I know it is," said the woman, unwrapping. "Everybody's told me."
cues.reason: Maintain the flatness of medical assessment.

cues.delivery: The woman delivers hard news with speed and clarity. No softening; she is explaining a necessity.
cues.from: "Then you'll want to hear this from me and not from a door," she said. "He's going in now. Not in the morning. Now. And you are not coming with him, and I'm going to tell you why, and then I'm going to go, because I haven't got time to be kind about it twice.
cues.through: "I promised him," said Jab.
cues.reason: Convey the urgency of medical protocol without melodrama.

cues.delivery: Jab's voice is firm but quiet. He holds his ground on the promise; it is a matter of honor.
cues.from: "I know," said the woman.
cues.through: "No," said Jab. "You don't understand. I promised him. He asked me if I'd be there and I said they'd have to carry me out."
cues.reason: Show Jab's resolve without making him argumentative.

cues.delivery: Jab speaks with absolute honesty. He admits his limitations to Tonk; the voice is gentle but unflinching.
cues.from: "I'll come after. It's twenty minutes and then I'll come after. That's not a maybe." He got his own hand round the small one properly, all of it. "They're going to look at your leg tonight, and there's going to be a doctor, and everybody in there is better at all of this than I am."
cues.through: Tonk absorbed this. Then, with a four-year-old's terrible instinct for the softest place available:
cues.reason: The admission of failure is a critical character beat.

cues.delivery: Tonk's accusation is sharp and factual. Jab accepts it without defensiveness.
cues.from: "You lied."
cues.through: "It's the only one."
cues.reason: Capture the child's direct perception of truth.

cues.delivery: Narrative voice is detached. Jab watches himself with a sense of dissociation.
cues.from: He let go of the hand. He made himself do it in one movement and not in stages, because stages would have been worse, and then he stood in the middle of a made road with his hands at his sides and watched two strangers lift his brother onto a stretcher and carry him in through a hole in an earth bank, and the light over the gate went out of his eyes for a moment and came back.
cues.through: He did not fall down. He noticed that with a certain distant surprise.
cues.reason: Reflect the numbness after emotional release.

cues.delivery: Internal monologue is rhythmic and heavy. The weight of the cord's history is felt in the pacing.
cues.from: Jab put his hand up under his collar. The cord had been there for four years. It had been there through nine days of a fish run, and a summer on a jam, and a bridge, and a gravel bar with his brother's blood on his hands, and sixteen days of road, and he had not once, since he was thirteen years old, gone to sleep without the small hard warmth of it lying in the hollow of his throat.
cues.through: He lifted it over his head and put it in a stranger's glove.
cues.reason: Convey the physical and emotional significance of the object.

cues.delivery: The surrender is quiet. Jab's voice in thought is blank and wonder-struck.
cues.from: It weighed nothing at all. That was the thing he had never noticed. He watched it go into a small bin with a clamp on it, and watched a man tie a paper tag to the handle and write on the tag, and he stood there in the road with his collar open and one hand still up at the place where it had been, and he thought, with a kind of blank wonder: well. Now I've got nothing at all.
cues.through: Then they hosed him down.
cues.reason: Emphasize the loss of identity through silence.

cues.delivery: Otto's voice is exhausted collapse. Jab's response is minimal acknowledgment.
cues.from: "Oh," said Otto, two places down, in a voice of total collapse.
cues.through: "Yes," said Jab.
cues.reason: Show the shared exhaustion of survivors.

cues.delivery: Callie's voice is flat and observational. She speaks as if reading a weather report about herself.
cues.from: Above them there was a light in a fitting behind a cage of wire. It was small and flat and white and it had no flame in it anywhere, and it did not move and it did not flicker, and Jab looked up at it and thought about a boy holding a hand out flat for snow at the top of a ridge and saying thousands.
cues.through: "I know," she said. "Your brother said it about ninety times."
cues.reason: Maintain the detached tone of someone who has seen too much.

cues.delivery: Hallet's voice is procedural and weary. Jab's responses are short and factual.
cues.from: "Ivor Hallet," he said, through the window. "I'm going to do this in the order it's got to be done in, and I'd ask you to let me, because out of order means starting again and it's the eleventh hour. Persons in party."
cues.through: "Yes," said Hallet, writing. "I'm sorry, sir. It's only a column."
cues.reason: Reflect the bureaucratic nature of the interaction.

cues.delivery: Hallet explains with clarity. Jab's internal reaction is silent calculation.
cues.from: "Declaration of capability," said Hallet, and laid a buff card on the ledge inside the window, and did not push it through.
cues.through: "Right," he said. "Give me the card."
cues.reason: Convey the weight of the 'bill' without emotional outburst.

cues.delivery: Jab's internal voice is searching. He struggles to find the right words for his capability.
cues.from: He wrote Flame, and then, because it was not the whole truth, he added: that's what they'd have said at home. I don't know what you'd say here.
cues.through: Then he sat with the pencil over the empty space for a long time.
cues.reason: Show Jab's uncertainty about how he fits into this new world.

cues.delivery: Jab writes with precision. The description of the knife is functional and honest.
cues.from: One shape. It's a fish knife — heavy, fat in the belly, hook on the end. I've had it four years. I can hold it all day and I can light it when I need it sharp, and the light sticks at the belly every time and always has.
cues.through: He read it back. Then he turned the card over, because there was no room left on the front, and wrote on the back:
cues.reason: Maintain the factual tone of the capability declaration.

cues.delivery: Jab writes about his second ability with caution. He is precise about what it does and doesn't do.
cues.from: There's a second thing and I haven't got a word for it.
cues.through: It does not touch his leg. I want that written down, because somebody's going to ask me and the answer's no. It has never gone within a hand's breadth of the bone and it never will.
cues.reason: Reflect the uncertainty and limitation of this power.

cues.delivery: Hallet's question is direct. Jab's answer is firm and factual.
cues.from: "This second thing. Has anybody taught you anything about it?"
cues.through: Hallet laid the card down on the desk in front of him, face up, square to the edge.
cues.reason: Show the uniqueness of Jab's situation.

cues.delivery: Jab speaks with quiet resolve. He is not asking for permission but for direction.
cues.from: "Most people haven't just handed you a piece of paper saying they can't do the only thing on it," said Jab, and Ivor Hallet made a small sound and wrote something in his book that Jab could not see.
cues.through: "That's not how—"
cues.reason: Capture Jab's shift from surrender to action.

pauses.after: Three hundred and forty paces, the girl had said, and Jab counted them, because his head would not do anything else.
pauses.reason: Completed thought on counting paces; allows listener to settle into the rhythm of arrival.

pauses.after: "That's one," said Tonk, with the last of what he had, and Jab laughed, and somewhere ahead of them a slab of steel began to come open in the side of an earth bank with a flat white lamp burning over it in the middle of the night.
pauses.reason: Light continuation after Jab's laugh and observation of the light.

pauses.after: There was a pause of about two seconds in which he understood that he had said exactly the right words in exactly the right order, and that the man in front of him had been going to get there anyway and had now got there faster, and that the carter with the broken chair on his cart had bought him about a minute and had known precisely what he was buying.
pauses.reason: Major emotional landing on Jab's realization that he has won a tactical victory; needs space to breathe.

pauses.after: Then she turned round and looked at Jab properly for the first time.
pauses.reason: Completed thought as the woman turns to look at Jab for the first time.
Preparation for the weight of Jab's endurance and sacrifice.

pauses.after: Something went across the woman's face that he could not read at all and did not have room to think about.
pauses.reason: Paragraph reset; shift from medical assessment to personal confrontation.
Light continuation after Jab's statement about being taken in without him.

pauses.before: better at all of this than I am
pauses.reason: Emphasis on Jab's admission of his own limitations compared to the doctors.

pauses.after: He let go of the hand. He made himself do it in one movement and not in stages, because stages would have been worse, and then he stood in the middle of a made road with his hands at his sides and watched two strangers lift his brother onto a stretcher and carry him in through a hole in an earth bank, and the light over the gate went out of his eyes for a moment and came back.
pauses.reason: Major emotional landing on the moment of separation; needs space for the weight of loss to land.

pauses.before: He let go of the hand
pauses.reason: Preparation for the critical action of separation; isolates the moment of release.
Emphasis on the object Jab is about to surrender; marks its significance.
Preparation for Jab's defense of the cord as something more than just a tool.

He watched it go into a small bin with a clamp on it, and watched a man tie a paper tag to the handle and write on the tag, and he stood there in the road with his collar open and one hand still up at the place where it had been, and he thought, with a kind of blank wonder: well. Now I've got nothing at all.
pauses.reason: Scene break equivalent (internal realization); pause after Jab's thought 'Now I've got nothing at all' before the next action.

pauses.after: Above them there was a light in a fitting behind a cage of wire. It was small and flat and white and it had no flame in it anywhere, and it did not move and it did not flicker, and Jab looked up at it and thought about a boy holding a hand out flat for snow at the top of a ridge and saying thousands.
pauses.reason: Light continuation on Jab's internal reflection about snow and thousands of lights.
Preparation for Jab's internal connection to the city lights and Tonk's earlier words.

pauses.after: "I know," she said. "Your brother said it about ninety times."
pauses.reason: Speaker reset; shift from Callie to the interaction with Hallet at the hatch.

pauses.after: Jab stood very still and watched the whole of the next year arrive in front of him on the other side of a pane of glass, laid out in its correct order, with a column for everything.
pauses.reason: Major emotional landing on Jab's realization of permanent displacement; needs space for the arithmetic of their future.
Emphasis on Jab's visualization of their permanent future; isolates the concept of time.
Preparation for Jab writing his rank; marks the word he chooses to represent himself.
Emphasis on Jab's description of his knife; isolates the functional nature of his power.

pauses.after: He did not look up for some time.
pauses.reason: Speaker reset after Hallet reads the card and looks up.
